title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Dust

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at what many consider Dickens's darkest and most ambitious novel.
Our Mutual Friend was his last completed work, and it is, in almost every sense, the most disturbing — a novel built on drowning, money, and the question of what a human life is actually worth.
Today we open with the fog and the dust — the novel's atmosphere, its moral landscape, and the astonishing confidence of its design.
Joining me are three brilliant readers, each of whom comes to this novel from a very different angle.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares above all about how great fiction is made — the architecture of sentences, the weight of a single image.
Eleanor's gift is making the technical feel thrilling, and I suspect she's been sitting on several observations about this novel for years.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a man who reads novels as moral dramas, stories about individual character tested by circumstance.
Edmund is suspicious of readings that flatten a novel into a political pamphlet, and he will say so, elegantly, whenever the temptation arises.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has recorded more classic audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive.
Oliver hears the rhythms of prose the way a conductor hears a score — and when he reads a passage aloud, something in it that you missed on the page suddenly becomes inevitable.
Let's begin with the question the novel puts to us before it's even properly started: what does the river mean?
The river in this novel is not scenery.
It is a character — possibly the most powerful one Dickens ever invented — and it does things to a story that no human character can do.
It swallows identities whole.
Consider the extraordinary passage where John Harmon discovers, reading a placard at Whitehall, that he is officially dead.
He rushes to see his own corpse — which is not his corpse at all — and what he realises, standing there, is this:

"I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me, and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide."
The same dark place, the same dark tide — that doubling is the whole novel in miniature.
Two men, one death, one river — and money at the centre of all of it.
What strikes me about that passage is the grammatical symmetry — Dickens writes himself into a kind of terrible balance.
Murdered for the money for which he would have murdered me — the syntax mirrors the moral equivalence.
Both men are potential killers, both potential victims, and the river simply sorts them without ceremony.
It's a kind of structural irony that Dickens builds into the very bones of the prose.
And that gothic atmosphere — the darkness, the tide — is doing moral work at the same time.
I think we must be careful not to let the atmosphere swallow the human being inside it.
What Dickens has achieved in that passage is something older than gothic atmosphere — it is the confrontation of a man with the fact of his own erasure.

John Harmon stands at Whitehall reading his own death notice — and the question that animates the entire novel follows from that moment: what does a man do when he has been given the freedom of not existing?
That is a question of character, not of capitalism.
Edmund is right that the human drama is supreme — but I'd argue the river earns its symbolic weight precisely because it keeps doing things.
Think of poor Gaffer Hexam — a man who has made his living fishing corpses from that same river — finally taken by it.
And Riderhood's response when the body is pulled out is so perfectly, grotesquely Dickensian — just four words:
"Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!"
Pure self-interest, not a flicker of pity — and Dickens delivers it with the comic timing of a man who knows exactly what he's doing.
And yet — against all that darkness and self-interest — there's a passage in the novel that feels almost like a creed.
Dickens steps back from the story to make a direct declaration about the nature of good and evil — and it is one of the most confident sentences he ever wrote.
He's been describing the Boffins — ignorant, unpolished, but guided by genuine duty and the desire to do right.
And then, in the narrator's voice, without apology or ornament, comes this:
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
That comma after 'Good' — the pause before 'never' — is not accidental.
It's Dickens conducting the sentence, making sure you feel the weight of that final word before it arrives.
That is Dickens at his most Johnsonian — the aphorism as moral assertion, delivered without hedge or qualification.
And notice that it arises not from one of his grand or educated characters, but from two people described as ignorant and unpolished.
Dickens has always understood — as the best moralists do — that goodness is not a property of refinement.
The Boffins carry a moral weight that all the fashionable Veneerings of this world could not muster between them.
Fog and dust on the outside — but underneath, a moral architecture of surprising clarity.
After the break, we'll go deeper into the characters who populate this landscape — and ask what Dickens means to do with his grotesques.

segments.title: Bella's Mercenary Heart: The Economics of Desire

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the moral architecture of Dickens's last completed novel — and today we're pressing on one of its most fascinating fault lines.
Money, marriage, and the question of whether desire itself can be corrupted by greed — or redeemed by love.
With me are three readers I trust absolutely to do this material justice.
Dr Eleanor Hartley — novelist, critic, and the person I most want beside me when a sentence is doing something extraordinary.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moral imagination personified, and a reader who refuses to let Dickens off any hook.
And Oliver Trevelyan — the actor and audiobook narrator whose ear for Dickens's prose rhythms is, frankly, unmatched.
Let's begin with the heart of the problem — John Harmon's confession about why he came back to England at all.
What strikes me immediately about Harmon's confession is how Dickens structures it as an act of self-interrogation — almost judicial in its form.
He doesn't simply explain himself. He puts himself on trial.
Listen to the accumulation of that word 'shrinking' — Dickens hammers it twice in quick succession.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That repetition of 'shrinking' is almost physical — you feel Harmon recoiling from the very inheritance that defines him.
And the chain of 'mistrustful' clauses that follows — mistrustful of the marriage, mistrustful of his father, mistrustful even of himself — it's a portrait of a man made of anxiety.
What Dickens is doing, architecturally, is making Harmon's psychological state inseparable from his relationship to money.
You cannot read his character without reading the economics of his upbringing.
Eleanor's right about the rhythm — but when I read that passage aloud, what hits me is the phrase 'mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious.'
He doesn't just fear the money. He fears what the money is doing to him in the act of wanting it.
That's the real engine of the whole Bella plot, isn't it?
The question is whether you can be contaminated by wealth simply by proximity to it — before you've even touched it.
And then the chapter on the deception — Dickens lays it all out with merciless clarity.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
'Meant to be harmless.' That's the saddest four words in the book.
Because of course it wasn't. Nothing involving his father's wealth ever was.
I think one must be careful not to let the economics swallow the moral drama entirely.
The passage Oliver reads is, yes, about wealth as a corrupting force — but it is equally a study in the weakness of will.
Harmon 'lapsed into the condition in which he found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
That is not a sentence about capitalism. That is a sentence about the human soul.
Dr Johnson might have written something very like it — indeed, probably did.
What Dickens understands, at his best, is that individual character is not merely shaped by circumstance — it must ultimately answer for itself.
Edmund, I don't entirely disagree — but I think the two things are the same thing in this novel.
What makes Harmon's dilemma so exquisitely constructed is that there's no clean exit.
Dickens states it baldly: 'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
Either path is a kind of moral damage. The money has already poisoned the field.
And that's exactly the trap Dickens lays — the soul must choose, but every choice has been pre-contaminated.
Can I drag us briefly to Mr Boffin, who provides the most magnificent comic counterweight to all this anguish?
There's a passage where Boffin goes off on charity patronage that is — I'm sorry — one of the funniest things Dickens ever wrote.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses — what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
'Up to his neck.' Dickens is drowning his own secretary in paperwork and finding it hilarious.
But the joke is also perfectly serious — it's Dickens anatomising the vanity of philanthropic display.
The title inflation is a form of moral inflation. No one is actually helping anyone.
Oliver has touched on something I find genuinely moving in this novel, which is the figure of Boffin himself.
When the whole deception is finally unravelled, Harmon says something that I think is among the most morally serious sentences in the book.
'I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin.'
'There are no words to satisfy me.' That is not rhetorical modesty. That is the genuine failure of language before genuine virtue.
Dickens was sometimes accused of sentimentality in his good characters. But Boffin earns every syllable of that tribute.
Because we have seen him tested — and seen him endure the test without complaint and without reward.
And against that portrait of Boffin's goodness, Dickens places Bradley Headstone — as if testing the opposite end of the moral spectrum.
The passage where Bradley sits through the night by the fire is extraordinary prose — almost expressionist in its technique.

'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
'The very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.' Dickens is making the body itself confess what the mind will not.
It's one of those moments where the narration goes somewhere only prose can go — not drama, not film. Pure prose.
What haunts me about that image is that Riderhood is watching. Vigilant.
The blackmailer and his victim, locked in a single room, neither speaking. It is almost classical in its unity.
And yet placed alongside Jenny Wren's vision — which is the counterpoint I keep returning to in this section — the contrast is devastating.
Jenny sees children who ask, simply: 'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!'
Bradley is also in pain — consuming, annihilating pain. But there are no bright children descending for him.
Grace, in this novel, is not universal. It seeks out the innocent and the humble.
I've read Jenny Wren's speech aloud many times, and it never gets easier.
She delivers it 'in a tone as though it were ages ago' — and the parenthetical is doing so much work.
She's a child speaking about her childhood as though from a great remove — which tells you everything about what her childhood cost her.
And then the vision itself — those children 'not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten,' who 'were never in pain.'
They are everything she is not. They are the negative of her existence.
And yet they come for her. The comfort is real, even if it's a vision.
That's what I find so remarkable about Dickens at moments like this — he doesn't sentimentalise the suffering away. He places the grace inside it.
That image of grace inside suffering feels like exactly the right place to pause and take stock.
We've moved from Harmon's fear of his own avarice, through Boffin's comic fury at the machinery of charity, to Bradley's annihilation — and Jenny's celestial counterpoint.
What this novel understands, as our guests have made vivid today, is that money is not simply a social force — it is a spiritual one.
We'll be back shortly to look at what happens when that force is finally, if provisionally, overcome.

segments.title: The Dust Heap and Social Rot: Boffin's Moral Gamble

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time in the river mud and the marriage market, but today we go to the dust heaps themselves — the moral and economic heart of the novel.
Boffin inherits a colossal fortune from old John Harmon — a man the novel calls, with magnificent contempt, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail.
And what happens next is a masterclass in what money does to human character — and what character can do to money.
Eleanor Hartley is with us — she'll be watching the architecture of how Dickens constructs the Boffins as moral touchstones.
Sir Edmund Leigh is here too, and I suspect he'll have something to say about virtue being its own reward — and whether the novel believes that.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has read these passages aloud more times than most of us have read them silently, will bring us close to the prose itself.
Eleanor, let's start with old Harmon's will — because the bequest to the Boffins is the pivot on which everything turns.
Yes — and Dickens does something structurally very bold here, which is to explain the old miser's logic retrospectively, from inside the narrator's omniscience.
We're not watching old Harmon decide to trust the Boffins — we're being told, after the fact, why a dead man once behaved as he did.
And that retrospective clarity is devastating, because it shows us a man who recognised virtue — and hated it — and rewarded it anyway.
The key phrase — and Dickens plants it so quietly — is this.
'He had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt.'
The miser's wealth — his supreme instrument of control — is rendered impotent by simple honesty.
That is Dickens making a structural argument about the moral limits of capital, embedded in a single subordinate clause.
I want to admire that reading, Eleanor, and in considerable measure I do.
But I'd resist the phrase 'argument about capital' — that makes it sound like a pamphlet, and it isn't.
What we have here is something far older and more profound: the recognition, by even a corrupted soul, that virtue is real.
Dickens says old Harmon mistrusted all who bore any resemblance to himself — that is a precise and terrible moral self-portrait.
The man knows what he is.
And the Boffins are trusted precisely because they are everything the old man is not — honest, true, unacquirable.
That is moral imagination at work in the novel, not social critique.
Edmund is right that it's not a pamphlet — but Eleanor is right that the architecture matters, and what I'd add is: listen to how the prose sounds.
'So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave them a good word, he had written their names down in his will.'
That 'So, even while' — repeated twice — is the rhythm of a man arguing against himself and losing.
Dickens builds the concession into the syntax itself.
And 'written their names down in his will' — such a plain, almost clerical phrase — lands with extraordinary weight.
So virtue is established — the Boffins are trustworthy, and the fortune is theirs.
And then Dickens immediately subjects that virtue to the most relentless comic pressure — the avalanche of supplicants that descends on Mr Boffin.
Oliver, this is your territory — you've read these passages aloud and I suspect you've enjoyed every word.
Enjoyed is something of an understatement.
The catalogue of charitable solicitations is one of the great comic set pieces of the novel — and it works because the contempt is so precise.
Dickens names the Duke of Linseed — and you must imagine the narrator's voice curling slightly around that title — who sends a lithographed letter by the hundred.
Here's the letter itself.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
'Large fat private double letter' — each adjective is a small outrage, and they accumulate beautifully.
The postscript — 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas' — is the punchline of the whole sequence.
Dickens calls it 'friendly' and 'thoughtful' — and the irony is so dry it could bleach linen.
And what I love is that the comedy isn't just entertainment — it's doing structural work.
The narrator asks, 'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
That phrase — dust for ocular use — echoes the novel's central metaphor perfectly.
The solicitations are not just fraudulent — they are a kind of dust thrown in the eyes, obscuring what is real from what is appearance.
Every noble institution, every lavish charity — they are literally made of paper, and Dickens tells us that directly: 'mostly lavish in the expensive articles of print and paper.'
Substance replaced by surface — that is the novel's great horror, and it starts right here.
I'm inclined to give Dickens a little more credit for the comedy itself, not merely as vehicle.
The individual beggars — catalogued in the very next passage — are a triumph of satirical taxonomy.
Consider the description of their so-called documents.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
That comparison is not political theory — it is wit of the highest order.
And the 'daughters of general officers, long accustomed to every luxury of life, except spelling' — I defy anyone not to laugh.
Dickens is observing human nature under pressure of want — and finding it, more often than not, absurd.
And yet — and Edmund will forgive me — there is something genuinely dark underneath the comedy.
The beggars of punctual business-habits, who announce they will be 'cold in death' at a quarter to one precisely if no postal order arrives — that is appalling as well as funny.
Dickens is not mocking desperation — he is mocking the language desperation learns to speak when it must compete for wealthy attention.
There's a category here — 'the inspired beggars' — musing over a fragment of candle, when an Angel whispers Boffin's name.
The mockery is surgical, but it doesn't quite cancel the image of that dying candle.
And lurking behind all of this — the corporate beggars, the inspired beggars, the noble earls with their lithographed appeals — is a second will.
Wegg has found it, and it reshapes everything.
Edmund, what does that will tell us about how Dickens has structured old Harmon's legacy?
The will Wegg produces is a document of magnificent, bitter economy.
Wegg describes it as 'regularly executed, regularly witnessed, very short' — and in that brevity lies the whole character of the man who wrote it.
Here is the core of it, as Wegg reads it.

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
'Quite enough for him' — spoken of a fortune others would kill for.
The contempt is total, and yet the bequest stands — because the old man's grudging respect for the Boffins could not be entirely extinguished, not even in revision.
Character, in this novel, outlasts even the intentions of the dead.
And what Dickens does with Wegg as the vehicle for revealing this is almost perverse — in the best sense.
Wegg is a grotesque, a fraudster, a man who sees the will as a lever — and yet through him we hear the document's strange poetry.
'He has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family' — that is an epitaph, and Dickens places it in the mouth of a rogue.
The contrast between the weight of those words and the cynicism of the man reading them is itself a structural argument about language and intention.
Dickens is always asking: who speaks, and what does that do to what is said?
Wegg performing the will is one of the great comic-sinister moments of the novel — and I'll tell you why it works as performance.
He calls it a 'sapprize' — a surprise — mangling the word as he mangles everything he touches.
His blandness, his buoyancy, his ghastly cheerfulness — 'I see I take you with me! Hear, hear, hear!' — is the cheerfulness of a man holding what he believes to be a weapon.
The comedy and the menace are completely inseparable.
And the pleasure Dickens takes in this character is palpable — every syllable of Wegg's speech is a small performance within the performance.
And then — after all of this — Dickens offers us a counterweight.
Not the dust heap, not the solicitations, not the will — but a simple supper.
Bella, Rokesmith, and old Wilfer — sharing a meal in a counting house, with the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles staring at them like a dull dragon.
Eleanor — what is Dickens doing with this moment?
He is doing something quite audacious — using fairy tale to make an argument about political economy.
Bella frames the supper herself — listen to this.

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
'Without their thunderous low growlings' — that phrase is doing everything.
The hobgoblins are possessiveness, territorial rage, the fear that something of mine has been taken — and they are absent from this meal.
What Bella and Rokesmith have is defined precisely by the absence of what the dust heap represents: acquisition, hoarding, the corrosion of human relationship by property.
I find myself in complete agreement with Eleanor, which happens rather less often than I might wish.
The narrator tells us it is 'by far the most delicious repast that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
And the uncongenial oddity of the surroundings — the iron safe, those brass knobs like a dragon's eyes — only makes it more delightful.
This is not social programme — this is the oldest human truth: that happiness is not in the accumulation of things, but in the quality of presence.
Dr. Johnson would have found nothing to surprise him here.
I want to close on 'R. Wilfer' — because Dickens uses the initial rather than the first name, and it's a small, perfect choice.
R. Wilfer is a man who has spent the entire novel gently, cheerfully overwhelmed by his domestic circumstances.
That he is here, at this table, listed among the happiest people — that is its own small redemption.
And the brass knobs of the safe staring 'like the eyes of some dull dragon' — the dragon is there, and it cannot touch them.
That is the whole novel in a single image.
The dust heap looms, the dragon stares — and three people eat a delicious supper and are happier than they have ever been.
Dickens earns that moment because he has shown us, with full satirical force, exactly what it is resisting.
Thank you to Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan.
In our next segment we'll follow the money further — into the Veneering circle, where everything glitters and nothing is solid.

segments.title: Harmon's Masquerade: Plot, Deception, and Narrative Sleight of Hand

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — paragraph by paragraph, character by character.
Today's segment goes to the heart of the book's most audacious structural gamble: John Harmon's masquerade.
The man presumed dead, moving through the novel under a false name, watching the world mourn him — and watching himself be mourned.
To help us pull this apart, I'm joined by three remarkable readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a clock — for the engineering behind the effect.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists the real subject of any great novel is moral character — not social machinery.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels for audio than perhaps any living person, and brings a performer's ear to everything he reads.
Let's begin with Dickens himself — because he does something extraordinary in the postscript to this novel.
He breaks the fourth wall entirely, and addresses the reader directly about the Harmon deception.
What's so striking about that postscript is how bracingly confident it is.
Dickens isn't apologising for the deception — he's defending it as a deliberate act of art.
He writes — and I want to read this precisely because the phrasing matters —

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
That doubling — concealing what he was suggesting, suggesting what he appeared to conceal — is the whole mechanism of the plot described in a single sentence.
He's not being coy with his readers. He's inviting them into the craft.
The passage is certainly remarkable — but I'd resist reading it as purely a statement about technique.
When Dickens asks his audience to concede him a little patience, he is asking something more fundamental than artistic trust.
He is asking them to believe that the world of the novel — its apparent cruelties, its deferred justice — will prove coherent in the end.
Harmon's masquerade, on that reading, is not a plot trick. It is a moral ordeal.
The man must prove himself worthy of the inheritance — and the identity — before he can claim either.
Edmund is right that it's a moral ordeal — but as a performer, what strikes me is that Dickens is also describing his own sleight of hand with complete transparency.
He's the conjuror who, after the trick is done, walks you through exactly how it was managed — and somehow the trick becomes more impressive, not less.
And the wonderful thing about trusting him, as he asks us to, is that the emotional groundwork was already being laid long before we meet Harmon-as-Rokesmith.
All those scenes with the Boffins — the memory of the boy — they do the moral work before the plot catches up.
Which brings us to those Boffin scenes — and the astonishing way Dickens builds our feeling for John Harmon through other people's memories of him.
Edmund, you've written about the moral weight Dickens places on childhood suffering. What do you make of these passages?
Mr Boffin is one of those characters in whom Dickens locates genuine goodness without sentimentality — or with very little of it.
He describes the old man's cruelties with the matter-of-fact directness of someone who has long since absorbed the shock.
The bonnet incident, told to Mortimer Lightwood, is almost comic in its specificity — and yet it isn't comic at all.
Boffin describes how old Harmon would send Mrs Boffin's black straw spinning across the yard.

"And once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn't thrown herself betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition — "Dropped her" — is Johnson's plain style turned to devastating effect. Two words. The weight of a life of service behind them.
The structural genius of that exchange is that Boffin is establishing his own credentials as a witness — and therefore as a moral authority in the novel.
He's telling Lightwood — and us — why his grief for the boy is trustworthy. He paid for it.
And then the memory of the child at seven — that's where the novel really breaks your heart.
The scanty travelling clothes, the scanty box — that double use of 'scanty' is doing enormous work.
It isn't describing poverty abstractly. It is measuring — with absolute precision — the smallness of what this child was allowed to take with him into the world.
I've read that passage aloud — recorded it — and I can tell you it is almost impossible to stay composed through Mrs Boffin's words at the fire.
Boffin describes how Mrs Boffin kneels at the fire, warms her hands, and rubs the child's cheeks — and then the tears come.

"Seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
"The wide wide world" — with that doubling — is the language of a folk song, of a ballad. Dickens is reaching for something older than the novel.
And then: "he rests his heart against her bosom, and looks up at both of us, as if it was in pain — in agony." That look haunts the whole book.
What I find most affecting is the decision Boffin reports the couple making — not to wish for a child of their own.
Mrs Boffin says: "We might both of us die, and other eyes might see that lonely look in our child."
It is a renunciation born entirely of love for a child not their own — and it is wholly convincing.
This is the moral imagination working at full stretch. Not a programme. A human being making an irreversible choice out of grief and tenderness.
And yet that grief doesn't calcify — it becomes the source of something generous. Mrs Boffin's proposal to adopt an orphan, to name him John Harmon.
Eleanor — that proposal seems to do something very strange in the architecture of the novel.
It does something almost uncanny — because of course John Harmon is not dead. He is about to walk into the Boffins' lives as their secretary.
So when Mrs Boffin says — and let me read this carefully —
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him" —
— we are watching Dickens lay a trap of the most delicate kind.
The name John Harmon is about to be both given away to a stranger and simultaneously reclaimed by the man it belongs to.
Identity in this novel is not fixed. It is fluid, transferable, contested — and in some cases, secretly preserved.
There's something almost liturgical about naming a child after the dead — which is exactly what Mrs Boffin proposes.
And Dickens lets that ritual comfort her — while the reader who suspects Rokesmith knows it is both touching and gently, quietly absurd.
She says herself: "Say it's only a whim" — and that little qualification is heartbreaking precisely because it isn't only a whim.
It is the whole novel's central act of reparation stated in miniature — goodness reaching across death to find a child to shelter.
Oliver puts it well. And I'd add that this quality of goodness-persisting-through-loss is what distinguishes the Boffins from virtually every other wealthy character in the book.
Money, in this novel, tends to corrupt or to reveal corruption. The Boffins are the exception — and that exception requires this backstory to be credible.
Without the child in the shivering wind and the weeping woman at the fire, we would not believe in Mrs Boffin's impulse to adopt. With them, we cannot disbelieve it.
Before we move on, I want to bring in one more passage — one that seems at first to belong to an entirely different register of the novel.
High above the city streets, on a rooftop, Riah the moneylender has laid out a carpet for two women — Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren.
Oliver — you have a feeling for the way Dickens shifts key in a passage like this.
That rooftop scene is one of those moments where Dickens essentially stops the novel to let you breathe.
Everything below is mud and money and deception — and then, there is this.
The narrator describes it with this exquisite gentle precision:

"Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet... they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces; Jenny with the sharper; Lizzie with the more perplexed."
That tripling — both pored, both attentive, Jenny sharper, Lizzie more perplexed — is the rhythm of a painter laying in light.
And then those old chimneys 'twirling their cowls and fanning themselves' — it's comic, it's pastoral, it's utterly itself.
What that scene shares with the Boffin passages is that both create enclosed worlds of tenderness inside a novel full of transaction and violence.
The carpet Riah spreads is an act of hospitality — quiet, unremarked, not performed for anyone's approval.
And that connects, structurally, back to the Boffins warming the child at their fire — small, private acts of shelter in a cold novel.
Dickens keeps returning to that image — a fire, a carpet, an outstretched hand — as the counter-grammar to the world's cruelty.
The counter-grammar to the world's cruelty — I think that's the phrase we'll carry with us into the next part of the conversation.
We've been looking at how Dickens engineers Harmon's disguise — not just as a plot mechanism but as a moral and emotional architecture.
Coming up, we'll turn to what the masquerade costs — what it means for a man to watch himself be mourned, and to defer his own identity for love.

segments.title: Laughter in the Shadows: Dickens's Comic Universe

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart sentence by sentence to find out how it works and why it endures.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the novel's most distinctive qualities: the way Dickens uses comedy — not as decoration, but as a kind of moral X-ray.
With me today are three guests who bring very different lenses to this extraordinary book.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — alert to every spring and gear.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's true business is the testing of individual character — and who will tell us if we're being too clever by half.
And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive, and he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because the comedy in this novel starts almost immediately, with one of the most brilliantly sustained metaphors Dickens ever wrote.
It does, and it arrives with that particular Dickensian confidence that takes your breath away.
Twemlow is introduced — and I use that word loosely — not as a man but as a piece of furniture.
The narrator calls him, without any apology whatsoever, "an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors."
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
Now — Lord Snigsworth.
Dickens doesn't need to do anything else with that name.
The contempt is already baked into the syllables.
But what kills me every time I perform this passage is the geometry that follows — Twemlow being pulled out, leaf by leaf, further and further from the centre.
The more socially useful he becomes, the more he is literally marginalised.
It's a comic diagram of exactly how society works — and it's funnier than any joke I've ever been asked to tell.
And the genius is that Dickens sustains the metaphor with absolute structural rigour — he doesn't let it wobble.
"Sometimes, the table consisted of Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, of Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his utmost extent of twenty leaves."
That triple repetition of 'sometimes' — it's entirely technical, the way a poet uses anaphora.
Dickens is using the structural device of accumulation to enact the very social process he's describing.
Each repetition adds another layer of exploitation, and the sentence itself becomes the dining table, extended.
I find it almost unbearably clever — and I mean that as the highest praise.
One mustn't lose sight of Twemlow himself, though — because beneath the metaphor there is a genuine human figure, and a rather touching one.
He is described as being kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street when not in use.
The comedy is there, yes — but so is something rather melancholy about a man whose entire existence is defined by his availability to others.
Dr. Johnson observed that the most corrosive satire is that which makes us laugh and then makes us ashamed of laughing.
That is precisely what Dickens achieves with Twemlow — and he achieves it in a single paragraph.
Edmund has put his finger on something I've always felt in performance but struggled to articulate.
The laugh is always available, but the sadness is always underneath it, and a good reader has to hold both at once.
Which brings me to Eugene Wrayburn — who is an entirely different kind of comedy, much darker and stranger.
Eugene is funny because he performs indifference with such virtuosity that you're not sure whether it's armour or whether it's simply the truth about him.
He says to Mortimer — and I want to read this because nothing I could paraphrase does it justice —

"You know how dreadfully susceptible I am to boredom. You know that when I became enough of a man to find myself an embodied conundrum, I bored myself to the last degree by trying to find out what I meant."
"An embodied conundrum."
That phrase does so much work — it's self-deprecating and self-dramatising simultaneously, and Eugene deploys it with the timing of a comedian who knows exactly how long to let the silence sit.
What strikes me technically is what Dickens does with the nursery rhyme at the end of that speech.
Eugene says his reply to the riddle runs — and I'll read exactly what Dickens gives him —
"No. Upon my life, I can't."
Two words, then four.
After all that elaborate verbal architecture — the conundrum, the boredom, the nursery form — Dickens brings it down to something almost childlike in its brevity.
The deflation is the point — and it tells us something true about Eugene, that underneath all the wit, there really is a kind of blankness he can't account for.
I want to push back very gently on the idea that Eugene's self-presentation is merely comic.
There is something morally serious at stake in a man who has declined to discover what he means — who has, as Dickens puts it, "given it up."
Burke would have recognised the type — the man of gifts who refuses the discipline of purposeful life and mistakes his own ennui for profundity.
The comedy is real and it is brilliant — but Dickens is also indicting a certain kind of educated idleness.
And we should not let Eugene's charm seduce us into missing the indictment.
And then there's a passage where the comedy recedes almost entirely — when we arrive at John Harmon's confession and the plot he devised to test Bella.
This is one of those moments where the novel shifts register completely, and Dickens asks us to take a very strange narrative device seriously.
Harmon says — and the language here is careful to the point of being almost painful —
"the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella."
"Proving Bella" — two words that carry the entire moral weight of the novel's marriage plot.
What Dickens is doing structurally is asking us to believe that a man would fake his own death to assess a woman's character — and making it feel not monstrous but almost tender.
The anxiety about money corrupting love — "the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil" — is doing all the emotional justification.
The passage matters because it illuminates the moral timidity Dickens explicitly names — a man whose childhood made him afraid to trust.
Harmon's scheme is not a manipulation in the cynical sense — it is the act of a man desperate to find out whether goodness is real in the world that destroyed his father.
That, to my mind, is the serious business of the novel — and it connects to the passage where young Charley Hexam confronts Bradley Headstone.
There the language of accountability — gratitude, responsibility, suspicion — is devastating precisely because it is spoken by a boy who has tried to build himself by his own effort.
Charley's confrontation with Headstone is one of the places where the comedy has entirely burned away, and what's left is something almost Jacobean in its intensity.
Charley says — and the rhetoric here is extraordinarily controlled —
"You know that I took you with me to his chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of him, and made myself responsible for my opinion of you."
Notice the construction: 'my opinion of him' and 'my opinion of you' — two different opinions in one sentence, both now compromised.
Charley has staked his reputation on vouching for a man who may be a violent criminal, and the sentence enacts that double exposure with extraordinary economy.
Then he ends with 'Is that your gratitude to me, Mr Headstone?' — and suddenly we're back in the world of social obligation, but now it's lethal.
I've performed that scene, and I can tell you it is ferociously difficult to pitch correctly.
Charley is both wronged and wrong — he's been used, but he's also used others.
The hedged syntax of the opening — 'If you had any part — I don't say what' — is Dickens showing us a boy who knows more than he dares to say.
And that kind of moral dread — the suspicion one cannot quite bring oneself to speak aloud — is perhaps the darkest note in a novel that keeps finding darkness underneath its laughter.
That phrase — darkness underneath its laughter — might serve as an epigraph for everything we've discussed today.
From Twemlow the dining table to Eugene's embodied conundrum, from Harmon's agonised scheme to Charley's terrible confrontation — the novel refuses to let comedy and tragedy occupy separate rooms.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan for a conversation that has genuinely deepened my sense of how this astonishing novel is built.
We'll be back next time with another corner of Our Mutual Friend — until then, keep reading.

segments.title: Redemption and Ruin: The Transformation of Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, scene by scene, to find out what makes it extraordinary.
Today's segment is called Redemption and Ruin: The Transformation of Our Mutual Friend.

We're looking at a cluster of passages that each, in their different ways, ask the same question: can a human being be remade — by love, by circumstance, by the sheer stubborn force of another person's faith?
With me today are three readers whose company I trust completely for this conversation.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens like an architect studying a cathedral — for the load-bearing structures hidden inside.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that the moral imagination of a novelist matters more than any social thesis — and he'll hold that line today, I suspect, with characteristic elegance.
And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive, and brings to every text the performer's ear — the sense of exactly where the pause should fall and why.
Let's begin with what might seem the humblest of our passages — a few sentences Lizzie Hexam speaks about a dying child, surrounded by drunkenness from birth.
What strikes me immediately about that passage is how Dickens loads the word 'cradle' — and then immediately undercuts it.
Lizzie's line is almost unbearably concise.
She says — and this is the whole weight of the novel's social conscience delivered in a single breath —
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthetical — 'if she ever had one' — does something structurally extraordinary.
Dickens lets Lizzie correct her own metaphor mid-sentence, and in doing so, reaches beneath the sentiment into something far colder and more devastating.
The cradle — that image of innocence and nurture — is taken away even as it's offered.
Eleanor is quite right about the syntactical sleight of hand, though I'd want to resist reading it purely as social argument.
What interests me is that Lizzie delivers this speech to Charley — her brother, who has climbed out of exactly this world and is already half-ashamed of where he came from.
Dickens is testing character here — not describing poverty, but asking what kind of moral fibre a person brings to the sight of suffering.
Notice that the father is described as 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober' — but the very next clause adds, 'a good workman too, at the work he does.'
That qualification is morally scrupulous — and it is Lizzie's character, not Dickens's programme, that supplies it.
She will not flatten a man into a case study, even a broken one.
What Edmund says about Lizzie's scrupulousness is exactly right — and when you read this passage aloud, that moment lands like a held note.
You build through the misery — the dead mother, the drink, the wretchedness — and then Lizzie simply says he's a good workman.
The audience — if you trust them, if you don't rush it — will feel the whole complexity of that in half a second.
The great performers' secret is that Dickens has already done the timing for you, if you follow his grammar.
That dash before 'if she ever had one' — it's a stage direction, not punctuation.
That image of Dickens as a writer of stage directions hidden in punctuation — I want to keep that in mind as we move to quite a different kind of transformation.
Edmund, you've been looking at Sloppy — a character who is being dressed up, literally remade by Mrs Boffin's kindness — and the results are not quite what tailoring science intended.
One must approach Sloppy with the appropriate gravity, which is to say, none whatsoever.
Dickens is here in full comic flight — but the comedy is doing serious work about the gap between intention and reality when wealth and poverty meet.
The tailor has received personal instructions from Rokesmith to conceal Sloppy's buttons.
The result, as Dickens puts it — and I find the classical allusion quite perfect —
'he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.'
Argus of the hundred eyes — a monster of classical mythology, deployed against a waistcoat.
The bathos is deliberate — and it tells us that the forms of respectability, when imposed on a body that doesn't fit them, become a kind of absurd spectacle.
What I love about that passage as a piece of prose architecture is the escalation — Dickens just keeps adding garments to the disaster.
The trousers hitching up at the ankles, bagging at the knees; the coat-sleeves retreating up the arms; and then, crowning all, that 'yawning gulf at his waistband.'
It reads like a slapstick routine, but the narrative voice keeps its own dignity intact — which is the key to why it works.
The phrase 'some special powers with which his legs were endowed' is a masterpiece of mock-heroic dead-pan — the legs are treated as having independent agency, blameless, almost gifted.
Sloppy himself is never humiliated in our eyes, only in the eyes of fashion — because Dickens's affection for him is clear in every word.
I once spent forty-five minutes working out how to read 'the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted' — about the hatband with the black bunch — and I still think I got it wrong.
It requires a kind of appalled solemnity — as though the narrator has been genuinely undone by a piece of millinery.

But what Edmund and Eleanor are circling is the deeper thing: Sloppy is being given entry into a world that doesn't quite fit him — and Dickens makes you feel the warmth of that gesture even as he laughs at the result.
The comedy never cancels the kindness — and that's the tonal tightrope Dickens walks in this novel again and again.
That tonal tightrope leads us straight to the passage I find most searching in this whole group — Lizzie's declaration of love for Eugene Wrayburn.
Edmund, this is yours — and it is about as far from the comedy of Sloppy's buttons as this novel gets.
This passage moves me every time — and I say that as someone not easily moved by what is sometimes called 'pure feeling' in fiction.
Lizzie is speaking in the third person — describing a lady rich and beautiful, when she means herself — and the indirection is not evasion but a kind of painful dignity.
She acknowledges that she knows Eugene has failings — 'she thinks they have grown up through his being like one cast away, for the want of something to trust in, and care for, and think well of.'
That is a precise and generous psychology — not the blindness of infatuation, but a considered account of a man who has lacked a moral anchor.
And then comes the great speech.

'Only put me in that empty place, only try how little I mind myself, only prove what a world of things I will do and bear for you, and I hope that you might even come to be much better than you are, through me who am so much worse, and hardly worth the thinking of beside you.'
The triple 'only' — anaphora, classical rhetoric — drives the speech forward like a tide.
And then that breathtaking self-abasement at the end: 'through me who am so much worse.'
She is not humbling herself out of weakness — she is offering her love as an act of transformative faith in another human being.
Edmund has named the anaphora, and he's right — but I want to push on the tense of 'I hope.'
Not 'I know,' not 'I believe' — only 'I hope.'
Dickens does not let Lizzie be sentimental about Eugene's redemption — she offers everything and claims only hope as her certainty.
That restraint is what gives the speech its moral weight — it's the structure doing what the sentiment alone could never do.
Reading that speech aloud — every time, without exception — I have to pause before 'I hope.'
Because the accumulation of those three 'onlys' has built such momentum that Dickens has to brake it — and the braking word is hope.
Eleanor is absolutely right that this is the architecture of the sentence doing the emotional work.
A lesser novelist would have written 'I know' — and the whole thing would have collapsed into wishing.
Transformation rooted in hope rather than certainty — that feels like a keynote of the whole novel, doesn't it.
Which makes our final passage all the more interesting — because Silas Wegg is planning a very different kind of transformation: turning blackmail into an empire.
Wegg is one of Dickens's supreme comic villains — and this passage is his masterpiece of self-delusion dressed as strategy.
The language is a parody of legal and parliamentary procedure — all those 'That, he would beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner' repetitions.
Wegg has dressed his greed in the costume of due process — which Dickens understood was precisely what the Circumlocution Office and its kind did every day.
But what makes this passage genuinely dark — beneath the comedy — is the phrase that ends it.
'He should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
Moral bondage.
Dickens uses the language of slavery without flinching — and he means us to feel the full weight of it against everything the novel has been saying about redemption and freedom.
The contrast with Lizzie's speech is almost schematic — Lizzie says 'only try how little I mind myself'; Wegg says extract everything, down to the last fraction.
But what I find brilliant as a piece of craft is that single word Wegg proposes as his price —
'Halves!'
One exclamation mark — and Dickens has captured the whole spirit of predatory capitalism in a single monosyllable.
And then of course Wegg immediately wonders whether it should be two-thirds, or three-fourths — greed being congenitally incapable of sufficiency.
The escalation is comic, but underneath it is something genuinely repellent about a mind that cannot stop dividing up the world.
I have read Wegg aloud many times, and the great pleasure — the guilty pleasure — is that the prose gives you the rhythm of a man in love with his own eloquence.
He calls Venus his 'comrade, brother, and partner' — three times, four times — and every repetition is Wegg reassuring himself that his scheme is solid and his alliance is real.
Set against Lizzie's 'only put me in that empty place' — that absolute selflessness — Wegg's language is revealed as the opposite: a total inability to imagine anyone else's worth at all.
One offers herself; the other offers slavery.
One offers herself; the other offers slavery — I think that's the beating heart of this segment.

From a child who perhaps never had a cradle, to a woman who offers to fill an empty place, to a man who wants to fill his pockets — Dickens has arranged these passages like movements in a moral symphony.
Eleanor, Edmund, Oliver — this has been extraordinary.
We'll be back with another segment very soon — and until then, as always, the novel rewards every return visit.
We've spent this episode following the river — its bodies, its money, its moral ambiguities.
And we arrive, at last, at a moment of reckoning — accusation, confession, and the terrible weight of what the river gives up.
Eleanor, you've been watching Gaffer Hexam from the very first pages — what is Dickens doing with that opening image of money pulled from the dead?
That opening image is one of the most compressed moral statements in the novel.
Gaffer comes up from the water — arms wet and dirty — and he washes them over the side.
And then, listen to what Dickens does with the money itself — the ritual of it.
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket."
Three identical gestures, in perfect series — chink, blow, spit — like a liturgy performed over a corpse's coin.
Dickens is encoding the entire moral architecture of the novel in a single paragraph.
The money is tainted — everyone knows it — and yet the ritual of luck is performed anyway.
And what makes it unforgettable as a performance is that hoarse voice — "for luck."
It's not a boast. It's not a prayer, exactly. It's something older and grimmer — a superstition that knows itself to be obscene.
When I read that passage aloud, I slow down for those three beats — chink, blow, spit — because the rhythm IS the meaning.
Each repetition is another nail. By the third, you feel something close to nausea.
And then the novel spends the rest of its considerable length asking — what happens to men who do such things?
Which brings us to the accusation — and it is a remarkable scene of character confrontation.
Riderhood steps forward — a man of no virtue whatsoever — and delivers, with absolute certainty, this indictment.
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body.
The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
That final repetition — "his hand and no other" — is prosecutorial in its ferocity.
And yet it comes from Riderhood — a man we cannot trust, whose motives are entirely self-serving.
Dickens forces us to attend to a truth delivered by a thoroughly unreliable vessel. That is a precise moral discomfort, and it is entirely deliberate.
Yes — and the discomfort is doubled by what Riderhood claims Gaffer actually said.
Because Riderhood doesn't just accuse — he reconstructs the alleged confession in full, with theatrical precision.
He gives us Gaffer's voice. And those words are devastating — listen.
"There was foul play then. I done it for his money. Don't betray me!"
Three short sentences. Subject, motive, plea. The entire confession fits in eleven words.
Whether it is true or fabricated — and Dickens keeps us suspended on that wire — the economy of the language is shattering.
"Don't betray me" — those three words carry everything.
Fear, guilt, and — most terribly — the recognition that one has placed oneself entirely at the mercy of a man like Riderhood.
If Gaffer is guilty, he has built his house on the river's mud — and the river, as this novel insists, gives everything up in the end.
And there's something almost classical about it — hubris enacted on the water, nemesis arriving in the form of a man equally corrupt.
One might add that Dickens is quite unsparing here about the moral condition of the river world.
It is not that poverty excuses. It is that the river, in this novel, is a place where the soul is perpetually tested — and frequently found wanting.
Gaffer, if guilty, has made his bargain. Riderhood has made his own.
The novel refuses to apportion sympathy cheaply. That, to my mind, is its great seriousness.
The river gives everything up — money, bodies, confessions, secrets — and asks only that you reckon with what floats to the surface.
Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan — it has been, as always, a genuine pleasure to think alongside you.
For listeners joining us for the first time: this is Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the novel is inexhaustible, and so, we hope, are we.
Until next time.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just

      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.
